transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?
I feel like I’ve lost the drive to do anything or be around people. It’s just getting harder and harder to talk or care about things the way I used to.

When you feel this way, have you also been hearing or seeing things other people don’t, or strongly believing things that others say aren’t true? Or has it mainly been low mood and loss of interest without those experiences?

I don't hear or see things that aren't there, but I mostly just feel really blank and flat inside. But... I am pretty sure the ladies at church and the clinic nurses are watching me and talking in code when they glance over. It feels like they've been told to keep an eye on me.

When these feelings of being watched happen, are you also feeling clearly depressed most of the day, like sad, hopeless, or guilty? Or do the suspicious thoughts continue even when your mood is not especially depressed?

I'm not really sure how to describe it, and I haven't really thought about it that way. I don't feel particularly sad or guilty, just very blank and empty inside. But those feelings about people watching me are still there regardless.

Before you started feeling blank and losing motivation, did you ever have a period when hallucinations or strong suspicious beliefs were much more obvious or intense than they are now? Or have these symptoms always stayed mild while the loss of emotion and motivation became the main problem?

The blankness and losing my drive definitely came first, starting over two years ago right after I finished high school. The feelings about people watching me and talking in code only started recently, in the last couple of months. The loss of motivation has always been the main, ongoing struggle.

final_diagnosis.reason: The presentation is most consistent with residual schizophrenia: longstanding predominant negative symptoms (affective flattening, avolition, social withdrawal, reduced speech/engagement) with only mild, persistent positive psychotic symptoms (ideas of being watched/talked about in code) and no prominent hallucinations. Simple schizophrenia was considered because negative symptoms developed insidiously and were primary, but it is less likely because the patient does report psychotic symptoms, which argues against a purely simple deterioration pattern.
